chain.g: to hit, strike, make contact with
to meet with, come upon, fall in with
to fall; fall upon; hit; cut; hew

ety.text: Proto-Indo-European *kh₂eyd-der. Proto-Indo-European *kh₂id-néh₂-ti Proto-Germanic *hittijaną Old Norse hittader. Old English hyttan Middle English hitten English hit Inherited from Middle English hitten (“to hit, strike, make contact with”), from Old English hittan (“to meet with, come upon, fall in with”), from Old Norse hitta (“to strike, meet”), from Proto-Germanic *hittijaną (“to come upon, find”), from Proto-Indo-European *kh₂eyd- (“to fall; fall upon; hit; cut; hew”).

From Middle English hit (“it”), from Old English hit (“it”), from Proto-Germanic *hit (“this, this one”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱe-, *ḱey- (“this, here”). Cognate with Dutch het (“it”). More at it; also note 'it.

senses.d: To administer a blow to, directly or with a weapon or missile.
ex: One boy hit the other.
He tried to hit me but I dodged the blow and went out to plot revenge.

senses.d: To come into contact with forcefully and suddenly.
ex: The ball hit the fence.
Meanwhile the street boys kept up a shower of mud balls, many of which hit the Doctor, while the rest were distributed upon his assailants.

senses.d: To strike against something.
ex: I can't get anything to hit at that distance.

senses.d: To activate a button or key by pressing and releasing it.
ex: Hit the Enter key to continue.

senses.d: To kill a person, usually on the instructions of a third party.
ex: Hit him tonight and throw the body in the river.
FREDO: Mikey, why would they ever hit poor old Frankie Five-Angels? I loved that ole sonuvabitch.

senses.d: To attack, especially amphibiously.
ex: If intelligence had been what it should have been, I don't think we'd ever have hit that island.

senses.d: To affect someone, as if dealing a blow to that person.
ex: Their coffee really hits the spot.
I used to listen to that song all the time, but it hits different(ly) now.

senses.d: To manage to touch (a target) in the right place.
ex: I hit the jackpot.
You can't hit the high notes in that song!

senses.d: To switch on or switch off (lights).
ex: Somebody's been here! Hit the lights!

senses.d: To commence playing.
ex:
- I'd love to hear your band play.
- Hit it, boys!

senses.d: A blow; a punch; a striking against; the collision of one body against another; the stroke that touches anything.
ex: The hit was very slight.
So he the fam'd Cilician fencer prais'd, / And, at each hit, with wonder seem'd amaz'd.

senses.d: Something very successful, such as a song, film, or video game, that receives widespread recognition and acclaim.
ex: Marie Taglioni was another hit for Her Majesty's Theatre last season, and will be a hit again this season[…]

senses.d: A blow; a calamitous or damaging occurrence.
ex: His reputation took a hit when the new information came to light.

senses.d: An attack on a location, person or people.
A collision of a projectile with the target.
In the game of Battleship, a correct guess at where one's opponent ship is.
A match found by searching a computer system or search engine
A measured visit to a web site, a request for a single file from a web server.
ex: My site received twice as many hits after being listed in a search engine.

senses.d: An approximately correct answer in a test set.
The complete play, when the batter reaches base without the benefit of a walk, error, or fielder’s choice.
ex: The catcher got a hit to lead off the fifth.

senses.d: Very successful.
ex: The band played their hit song to the delight of the fans.

senses.d: It.
ex: But how hit was to come about didn't appear.
Now, George, grease it good, an' let hit slide down the hill hits own way.
